Chapter 49

Migrating a major: the routine, the record, and a dependency still on Svelte 4

sv migrate and its task-based migrations — one task per commit, @migration-task comments, and a MIGRATION_TASKS.md for what no tool can decide — with the record this project kept, every box resolved. What SvelteKit 3 removed and renamed, module by module and option by option; and how to read a component written for Svelte 4, each legacy construct with its runes replacement and the code that flags it.

By the end of this chapter

Run a major upgrade as a reviewable series of commits, resolve every finding with evidence, and read legacy Svelte without writing any.

A major version is a list of breaking changes and, these days, a tool that makes most of them for you. The skill is in the rest: knowing which changes the tool made, which it could not, and how to leave a record that the next person — or the next major — can trust. This chapter is the routine for a project that is on SvelteKit 2, and it is not Meridian’s history: Meridian was started on the 3.0 prereleases and moved to 3.0.1 in a single commit, by hand, so there is no run of nine commits in its log to point at. What it does have is the record the routine ends in — the tool run against a copy of the finished project, every finding resolved with evidence — and that is what the rest of the chapter reads. A course that claimed a history the repository does not have would be teaching you to trust a record you cannot check.

sv migrate has two kinds of migration. The newer ones are *task-based*: sveltekit-3 and app-state. The older ones — svelte-5, self-closing-tags, svelte-4, sveltekit-2, package, routes — are delegated to svelte-migrate@1, kept so old projects can move forward, and, in the documentation’s words, “no longer receive updates”. A task-based migration shows its tasks before it runs any; the *prerequisite* tasks always run, and the rest are chosen interactively or with --tasks. Run without IDs, --tasks lists them; --tasks all runs everything at once, which the documentation reserves for automation. The other options are plumbing: --cwd to run against another directory, --confirm to skip the last prompt in a script, --install <manager> or --no-install, and --files <glob> — an escape hatch that saves only matching files, which the documentation warns “can leave imports, configuration, or types inconsistent”.

Why one task per commit

Because a migration commit is reviewed by reading its diff, and nine tasks in one diff is a diff nobody reads. The documentation says it outright: run “one selectable task at a time and commit the result before starting the next one”, and — just as important — “do not expect a project to work after running only a few tasks”. The commits are for review, not for stopping half-way. When something breaks after the fourth, git bisect has nine small commits to choose from instead of one large one.

A minor release is a different job and needs none of this. SvelteKit 3.1.0 had no breaking changes, so there is no migration tool to run and no diff to review beyond the version numbers: bump the range in package.json, install so the lockfile follows, and run the gate. The gate is the evidence — verify type-checks, lints, tests, builds and drives a browser through the result — and a release that broke something the gate never reaches would be a gap in the gate, not a reason to trust the changelog less. Read the changelog all the same, because it says where the new behaviour lives: 3.1.0 added a CSP keyword family (chapter 47), a span for +server handlers (chapter 37) and a guard for a failing service-worker update (chapter 39), and moving Meridian from 3.0.1 to 3.1.0 touched them differently. The CSP keywords change nothing here, because Meridian collects no violation reports. The span does change what you see: the diagnostics table lists every recorded span, so /healthz and the route API now appear in it. The guard matters only on the path where a worker update fails, and there the reload now goes ahead.

The record: every finding resolved

What a task cannot decide safely it leaves in two places: @migration-task comments at the spot, and a MIGRATION_TASKS.md at the root listing the migrations that are “uncommon, context-dependent, or disproportionately difficult to automate safely”, each with the files worth a look. The file’s own instruction is to delete it when the work is done. Meridian has one because the tool can be run on a finished project too: it was run against a copy, the findings were resolved by hand, and the result is kept as docs/migration-sveltekit-3.md, with every box ticked and the evidence beside it.

The findings are deliberately broad, and the file says so — “may include files that do not require changes”. Eight of the twenty boxes here were false positives, and *not affected, because* is a resolution as long as the because is checkable. The header’s page.url finding was a read, never a write. The error(...) finding in the trip page was svelte-sonner’s toast.error. The one below is the most instructive: three forms flagged for hand-written name attributes, none of them remote forms.

The rule behind that task is strict — the migration guide says a hand-written name on a remote form “will cause the submission to be rejected” — so the check had to be real: each flagged <form> is plain HTML with an onsubmit that calls a command, and its name only groups radio buttons for the browser. Every actual remote form takes its attributes from fields.x.as(…) (chapter 18).

And the behaviour that changed under code that still compiles, which is where an upgrade actually bites. In this project each was met and answered: error() takes a message string, with extra properties as a third argument; handleError now receives *every* error, told apart by kind, and can set the status; json() and text() are deprecated for Response.json() and new Response(); goto rejects a URL that is not a route; page.url is readonly; delta exists only for popstate; preloadData can return an error result; a 204 has no body; a cookie with no path gets /; data-sveltekit-* attributes take false, not 'off'; a redirect off the site needs { external }; a link to the current page refreshes; a universal config wins over a server one; and the service worker is registered as a module.

Reading a dependency that is still on Svelte 4

Svelte 5 still compiles Svelte 4 syntax — a component without runes is in *legacy mode* — so a library written for 4 usually runs. You will read its source when it misbehaves, and every construct in it has a runes equivalent and a code that names it. No code in this project is written in legacy mode; this is a reading table.

Svelte 4 constructs, their runes replacements, and the code that flags each in runes mode
Svelte 4Svelte 5Flagged by
let count = 0 (implicitly reactive)let count = $state(0)non_reactive_update when a plain let is reassigned and read reactively
$: double = count * 2; $: { … }$derived(count * 2); $effect(() => { … })legacy_reactive_statement_invalid; run() from svelte/legacy is the migration’s stopgap
export let namelet { name } = $props()legacy_export_invalid
$$props, $$restPropslet props = $props(); let { a, ...rest } = $props()legacy_props_invalid, legacy_rest_props_invalid
on:click={…}, on:click|preventDefaultonclick={…}, and event.preventDefault() inside itevent_directive_deprecated; mixed_event_handler_syntaxes if both appear
createEventDispatchercallback propsdeprecated in the types; the migration script leaves it to you
<slot />, $$slots, <svelte:fragment>{@render children()}, snippet propsslot_element_deprecated; slot_snippet_conflict if mixed
<svelte:component this={X}><X /> — components are dynamicsvelte_component_deprecated
<svelte:self>the component imports itselfsvelte_self_deprecated
new App({ target }), $set, $on, $destroymount(App, { target }), $state props, unmountlegacy_component_creation; at run time component_api_changed, component_api_invalid_new
beforeUpdate, afterUpdate$effect.pre, $effect (and tick)lifecycle_legacy_only
SvelteComponent, ComponentType, ComponentEventsthe Component type; callback props instead of eventsdeprecated in the types: “SvelteComponent, the base class from Svelte 4, is deprecated in favour of the new Component type”
<script context="module"><script module>script_context_deprecated
<div /><div></div>element_invalid_self_closing_tag; npx sv migrate self-closing-tags

svelte/legacy is the bridge the svelte-5 migration reaches for when it cannot be sure: run for a $: it could not classify, createBubbler and handlers for forwarded events, the eight modifier helpers — once, preventDefault, self, stopPropagation, stopImmediatePropagation, trusted, passive, nonpassive — and asClassComponent / createClassComponent with the LegacyComponentType type for code that still says new Component(…). For a dependency you cannot change, compilerOptions.compatibility.componentApi: 4 makes new Component(...) keep working, at “a bit of overhead to each component”. Each is a way to finish migrating later; none is a way to write new code.

Turning a component into runes mode changes more than syntax, and these are the ones that surprise people. Props are not bindable unless declared with $bindable(). accessors and immutable are ignored. A class instance is not “auto-reactive” — only its $state fields are, and wrapping new Foo() in $state does nothing. ontouchstart and ontouchmove handlers are passive. An attribute that concatenates must be quoted. HTML the browser would repair is a compile error. Selectors inside :is(), :has() and :where() are scoped now. Whitespace between nodes collapses to one space and is trimmed at the edges of a tag. And children is a reserved prop name, because content between a component’s tags *is* the children snippet.

The two migrations this course made by hand

Two pieces of syntax changed under this project after it was written, and neither has a migration task, because both old forms still compile. {@const x = …} became the declaration tag {const x = $derived(…)} — twenty-seven of them across twenty components, and no {@const} left — for the placement rule and the computed-once value chapter 45 describes. And class:active={…} directives became class={['chip', { active }]} arrays — fifteen class arrays across ten components, no class: directive left — because one attribute that says everything about an element’s classes reads better than a list of directives, and merges with a class prop without string-building. The autofixer’s legacy checks and pnpm run lint:svelte keep both from coming back.

Checkpoint

  • You can run a task-based migration one task per commit, and say what --tasks, --files, --cwd, --confirm and --no-install do.
  • You can resolve a MIGRATION_TASKS.md finding with evidence, including the findings that are false positives.
  • You can name what replaced $app/environment, $app/stores, $service-worker, $env/*, $lib and resolveRoute.
  • You can read a Svelte 4 component and name, for each construct, its runes form and the code that flags it.
